units.title: Dimensionality and Geometry of Location
units.intro: Solids: prisms and pyramids (polyhedra), cylinder, cone, sphere. Nets fold to the surface. Views: front, side, top.

cards.title: 4.1.1 Plane figures, solids and polyhedrons
body: **Plane figures** (triangles, squares, circles …) have only length and width, so they are **two-dimensional (2-D)**. A **solid** has length, width **and** height, so it is **three-dimensional (3-D)** and occupies space. A solid is an enclosed part of space bounded by plane (flat) or curved surfaces.

A **polyhedron** (plural polyhedrons or polyhedra) is a solid bounded by **flat polygon faces only**. The faces meet in line segments called **edges**, and the edges meet at points called **vertices**.
- Cubes, prisms and pyramids are polyhedrons.
- Cylinders, cones and spheres are **not** polyhedrons: each has a curved surface.

A polyhedron is **regular** when all its faces are congruent regular polygons **and** the same number of faces meet at every vertex. Examples: the cube (6 squares) and the regular tetrahedron (4 equilateral triangles).

**Smallest polyhedron:** you need at least 4 faces to close up space, so 3 triangles can never make a polyhedron, but 4 triangles can (a tetrahedron), and one square with 4 triangles makes a square pyramid.

cards.title: Which solids are polyhedrons?
body: Dashed lines are edges hidden at the back. A solid is a polyhedron only when **every** face is flat.

cards.title: Prisms
body: A **prism** has two congruent, parallel faces called the **bases**; the other faces (**lateral faces**) are parallelograms joining corresponding sides of the bases. The edges joining the two bases are the **lateral edges**; they are all parallel and equal.
- A prism is named after its base: triangular prism, rectangular prism, pentagonal prism, hexagonal prism …
- **Right prism:** the lateral edges are perpendicular to the bases, so the lateral faces are rectangles. Otherwise the prism is **oblique**.

- A **rectangular solid** (cuboid) is a prism bounded by six rectangles; a **cube** is a rectangular solid bounded by six squares. A square prism is a cube only if its height equals the side of the square.
A **cross-section** of a prism is where a plane **parallel to the base** cuts the prism.

**Theorem 4.1:** every cross-section of a triangular prism is congruent to the base. **Theorem 4.2:** the upper and lower bases are congruent. **Theorem 4.3:** all cross-sections of any prism have the same area.
The union of the lateral faces is the **lateral surface**; lateral faces plus both bases make the **total surface**.

cards.title: A right triangular prism
body: The purple cross-section $DEF$ is parallel to the base, so $\triangle DEF \cong \triangle ABC \cong \triangle A'B'C'$.

cards.title: Pyramids and frustums
body: A **pyramid** has one polygon **base** and triangular **lateral faces** that meet at a common vertex, the **apex**. It is named after its base (triangular, square, pentagonal … pyramid).
- **Lateral edges:** where two lateral faces meet (from the apex to a base corner).
- **Altitude:** the perpendicular segment from the apex to the base; its length is the **height** $h$.
- **Slant height:** the altitude of a lateral face drawn from the apex (from the apex to the midpoint of a base edge).
- **Regular pyramid:** the base is a regular polygon and the foot of the altitude is the centre of the base. Then all lateral faces are congruent isosceles triangles.
A **tetrahedron** is a pyramid with a triangular base: 4 triangular faces, 3 meeting at each vertex.
If a plane parallel to the base cuts off the top of a pyramid, the part left is a **frustum**. Its two bases are similar polygons and its lateral faces are **trapezoids**.

cards.title: Parts of a rectangular pyramid
body: Height and slant height are different: the height goes straight down to the base (inside the pyramid), the slant height runs down the middle of a face. The slant height is always the longer one.

cards.title: Worked example: height, slant height and lateral edge
cards.problem: A regular square pyramid has base edge $12$ cm and height $8$ cm. Find the slant height and the length of a lateral edge.

steps.text: Draw the right triangle: apex, centre of the base, midpoint of a base edge. Its legs are the height $8$ and half the base edge $6$.
Now the right triangle: apex, midpoint of a base edge, a corner. Its legs are the slant height $10$ and half the edge $6$.

cards.answer: slant height $10$ cm, lateral edge $\sqrt{136} \approx 11.7$ cm

cards.title: 4.1.2 Cylinders, cones and spheres
body: A **cylinder** has two parallel, congruent circular bases and a curved **lateral surface** joining them. If the segment joining the centres of the bases (the **axis**) is perpendicular to the bases, it is a **right cylinder**. Every horizontal cross-section is a circle congruent to the base — just like a prism, which is why cylinder and prism share the volume rule "base area × height".

A **cone** has a circular base and a lateral surface that comes to a point, the **vertex**. The **altitude** (height $h$) goes from the vertex perpendicular to the base; the **slant height** $l$ goes from the vertex to the edge of the base. In a right cone $l^2 = r^2 + h^2$. A cone is to a cylinder what a pyramid is to a prism. Cutting a cone parallel to its base leaves a **frustum of a cone**.

A **sphere** is the set of all points in space at the same distance $r$ (the radius) from a fixed point $O$ (the centre). It is formed by rotating a semicircle about its diameter. A **great circle** is a cross-section through the centre (radius $r$); any other cross-section is a **small circle**.
A circle is flat (2-D); a sphere is solid (3-D). Do not mix them up.

cards.title: Height, radius and slant height
body: For the cone the height $h$, the radius $r$ and the slant height $l$ make a right triangle: $l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$.

cards.title: Cross-sections of a sphere
body: A cross-section at distance $s$ from the centre is a circle of radius $t$ with $t^2 = r^2 - s^2$ (Pythagoras). Its area is $\pi t^2 = \pi(r^2 - s^2)$ — the same as the area of a ring (**annulus**) between circles of radius $r$ and $s$.

cards.title: Worked example: cross-section of a sphere
cards.problem: A sphere has radius $13$ cm. A plane cuts it $5$ cm from the centre. Find the radius and the area of the cross-section.

steps.text: The radius of the sphere, the distance from the centre and the radius of the section form a right triangle: $t^2 = r^2 - s^2$.

cards.title: 4.1.3 Nets and views of solids
body: A **net** is a flat (2-D) figure that can be folded into a solid. Every face of the solid appears exactly once in the net, and no two faces overlap after folding.
- A cube has 6 square faces, so a cube net has 6 squares. There are exactly **11** different cube nets. A row of 4 squares with one square above and one below (anywhere) always works.
- A tetrahedron net is 4 triangles, for example one large triangle split into 4 by joining the midpoints of its sides.
- A cylinder net: two circles and a rectangle whose length is the circumference $2\pi r$. A cone net: a circle and a sector.
**Test a net:** pick one square as the bottom and fold the others up in your head. If two squares land on the same face, it is not a net (for example 6 squares in a row, or a $2 \times 3$ block).
A 3-D solid can also be described by its **views**: the **front view**, the **side view** (from the right) and the **top view** (plan), each drawn as a flat figure.
- Upright cylinder: front and side views rectangles, top view a circle.
- Square pyramid: front and side views triangles, top view a square with its diagonals.
- Cone: front view a triangle, top view a circle with its centre marked.

cards.title: Views of a solid made of cubes
body: Count squares: from the front you see an L of 3 squares; from the right only 2 stacked squares (the right-hand cube hides the left column); from the top 2 squares in a row.

cards.title: Euler’s formula
body: For every polyhedron (without holes) the numbers of faces $F$, vertices $V$ and edges $E$ satisfy
Prism with an $n$-sided base: $F = n + 2$, $V = 2n$, $E = 3n$. Pyramid with an $n$-sided base: $F = n + 1$, $V = n + 1$, $E = 2n$. In both cases $F + V - E = 2$.

cards.title: Worked example: using Euler’s formula
cards.problem: A polyhedron has $12$ vertices and $30$ edges. How many faces does it have?

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Verify Euler's Formula for a triangular prism ($$F = 5$$, $$V = 6$$, and $$E = 9$$). What is the value of $$F + V - E$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the variables**
For a triangular prism, we are given:
- Faces ($$F$$) = $$5$$
- Vertices ($$V$$) = $$6$$
- Edges ($$E$$) = $$9$$

**Step 2: Substitute the values into Euler's Formula**
The expression is $$F + V - E$$:
$$5 + 6 - 9$$

**Step 3: Simplify the expression**
$$11 - 9 = 2$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The value is **$$2$$**, which confirms Euler's Formula.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following three-dimensional solids is NOT a polyhedron?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the definition of a polyhedron**
A polyhedron is a three-dimensional solid bounded strictly by flat, polygonal plane surfaces.

**Step 2: Analyze the geometric shapes**
- Triangular prisms, square pyramids, and regular tetrahedrons are all bounded strictly by flat polygons (triangles, squares, rectangles). Thus, they are polyhedrons.
- A cylinder has a curved lateral surface and circular bases, which are not polygons. Thus, it is not a polyhedron.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The curved solid that is not a polyhedron is **A cylinder**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A cube has how many faces, edges and vertices respectively?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** A cube has 6 square faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

**Step 2:** Check with Euler's formula: F + V − E = 6 + 8 − 12 = 2.

**Step 3:** Answer: 6, 12, 8.

**Tip:** Euler's formula F + V − E = 2 holds for every convex polyhedron – use it to check counts.

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the definition of a polyhedron**
A polyhedron is a three-dimensional solid bounded strictly by flat, polygonal plane surfaces.

cards.title: 4.2.1 Coordinates in a plane
body: On a number line the distance between two numbers $a$ and $b$ is $|b - a|$, e.g. between $-3$ and $9$: $|9 - (-3)| = 12$ units.

Two perpendicular number lines, the **x-axis** (horizontal) and the **y-axis** (vertical), meet at the **origin** $O(0, 0)$ and make the **coordinate plane** (xy-plane). The axes divide the plane into four **quadrants**, numbered anticlockwise starting top-right.

To find the coordinates of a point $P$: drop a perpendicular to the x-axis (foot $M$, number $a$) and to the y-axis (foot $N$, number $b$). Then $P = (a, b)$. The first number is the **x-coordinate (abscissa)**, the second the **y-coordinate (ordinate)**. Order matters: $(4, 1) \ne (1, 4)$ — that is why it is called an **ordered pair**.
- Points on the x-axis have $y = 0$: $(4, 0)$. Points on the y-axis have $x = 0$: $(0, 9)$.

cards.title: Example 4.4: triangle P(0, 0), Q(5, 0), R(0, 12)
body: The legs lie on the axes: $PQ = 5$, $PR = 12$, and the angle at $P$ is a right angle.
**Area** $= \frac12 \times 5 \times 12 = 30$ square units. **Hypotenuse** $QR = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$, so the **perimeter** $= 5 + 12 + 13 = 30$ units.

cards.title: 4.2.2 Distance between two points
body: **Same horizontal line** ($y$ equal): distance $= |x_2 - x_1|$. **Same vertical line** ($x$ equal): distance $= |y_2 - y_1|$. Example: $P(2, 4)$, $Q(2, 10)$ → $PQ = 6$.
**General case:** for $P(x_1, y_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2)$ draw the right triangle $PRQ$ with $R(x_2, y_1)$. Then $PR = |x_2 - x_1|$ and $RQ = |y_2 - y_1|$, and Pythagoras gives
- The order of the points does not matter, because $(x_1 - x_2)^2 = (x_2 - x_1)^2$.
- Distance is never negative; take the positive square root.
- Write brackets around negative numbers: $2 - (-1) = 3$.

**Uses:** prove a triangle is isosceles (two equal sides), equilateral (three equal sides) or right-angled (converse of Pythagoras: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ for the longest side $c$); test collinearity (the two short distances add up to the long one).

cards.title: Why the distance formula works
body: The horizontal leg is the change in $x$, the vertical leg is the change in $y$; the distance is the hypotenuse.

cards.title: Worked example: distance and type of triangle
cards.problem: Do $P(3, 2)$, $Q(-2, -3)$ and $R(2, 3)$ form a triangle? If so, what type?

steps.text: Sum of the two shorter sides $\sqrt{50} + \sqrt2 \approx 8.49 > \sqrt{52} \approx 7.21$, so it is a triangle.
Check Pythagoras on the squares: $PQ^2 + PR^2 = 50 + 2 = 52 = QR^2$, so the angle at $P$ is $90°$.

cards.answer: Yes — a right-angled triangle (right angle at $P$)

cards.title: Worked example: isosceles triangle
cards.problem: Show that $P(-2, 3)$, $Q(3, 8)$, $R(4, 1)$ form an isosceles triangle.

steps.text: $PQ = QR$, so two sides are equal.

cards.title: Worked example: a point on the x-axis equidistant from two points
cards.problem: Find the point on the x-axis that is the same distance from $A(2, -5)$ and $B(-2, 9)$.

steps.text: A point on the x-axis is $P(x, 0)$.
Set the squared distances equal (no square roots needed): $(x - 2)^2 + (0 + 5)^2 = (x + 2)^2 + (0 - 9)^2$.

cards.title: 4.2.3 Midpoint of a line segment
body: The **midpoint** $M$ of $P_1P_2$ is the point of the segment halfway between the ends. Its coordinates are the **averages** of the end coordinates:
$$M = \left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)$$

**Why:** drop perpendiculars from $P_1$, $P$, $P_2$ to the x-axis ($R_1$, $R$, $R_2$). Parallel lines cut equal pieces, so $R$ is the midpoint of $R_1R_2$ and its number is $\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}$. In the same way $S$ on the y-axis gives $\frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}$.
- Horizontal segment $(x_1, y)$ to $(x_2, y)$: midpoint $\left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, y\right)$. Vertical: $\left(x, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)$.
**Missing endpoint:** if $M$ and $A$ are known, $B = (2x_M - x_A, 2y_M - y_A)$ — "double the midpoint, subtract the known end".
**Do not confuse:** distance **subtracts** and squares (gives a number); midpoint **adds** and halves (gives a point).

cards.title: Distance and midpoint formulas
body: Distance: subtract, square, add, square-root — the answer is a **number**. Midpoint: add and halve — the answer is a **point**.

cards.title: Worked example: find an endpoint from the midpoint
cards.problem: M(2, −1) is the midpoint of AB and A = (−3, 4). Find B.

steps.text: Step 3: check: midpoint of (−3, 4) and (7, −6) is (2, −1) ✔.

cards.title: Worked example: parallelogram from midpoints
cards.problem: $A(1, 2)$, $B(4, y)$, $C(x, 6)$ and $D(3, 5)$ are the vertices of a parallelogram taken in order. Find $x$ and $y$.

steps.text: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so $AC$ and $BD$ have the same midpoint.
Same slope through the common point $A$, so the three points lie on one line.

cards.title: Key formulas of coordinate geometry
body: **Distance** between $A(x_1, y_1)$ and $B(x_2, y_2)$: $AB = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$.
**Midpoint** of $AB$: $M = \left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)$.

**Slope** of $AB$: $m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ ($x_1 
e x_2$). Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is $-1$.
Example: for $A(1, 2)$ and $B(4, 6)$, $AB = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$, the midpoint is $(2.5, 4)$ and the slope is $\frac{4}{3}$.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Find the distance between the coordinate points $$P(2, 4)$$ and $$Q(2, 10)$$ using the Distance Formula.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Write down the Distance Formula**
$$d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$$

**Step 2: Substitute coordinate values**
Here, $$(x_1, y_1) = (2, 4)$$ and $$(x_2, y_2) = (2, 10)$$:
$$d = \sqrt{(2 - 2)^2 + (10 - 4)^2}$$

**Step 3: Simplify the expression**
$$d = \sqrt{0^2 + 6^2}$$
$$d = \sqrt{36} = 6$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The distance between the points is **$$6$$**.

cards.title: Transformations of the plane
body: A **transformation** of the plane is a one-to-one mapping of the whole plane onto itself: every point $P$ has exactly one **image** $P'$, and every point is the image of exactly one point (its **pre-image**).
In this unit: **reflection** (flip in a mirror line or a point), **translation** (slide) and **dilation** (enlarge or shrink from a centre).
- Reflections and translations keep every length and angle: the image is **congruent** to the figure. They are **rigid motions** (isometries).
- A dilation keeps angles and shape but multiplies all lengths by the scale factor $r$: the image is **similar** to the figure.

cards.title: 4.3.1 Reflection
body: A **reflection in a line $l$** maps a point $P$ to the point $P'$ such that $l$ is the **perpendicular bisector** of $PP'$: $PP' \perp l$ and $P$ and $P'$ are the same distance from $l$, on opposite sides. A point on $l$ is its own image.
Like a mirror: your image is as far behind the mirror as you are in front of it.
- A reflection keeps distances: $A'B' = AB$. It reverses orientation (clockwise becomes anticlockwise).
- A figure is **symmetric about $l$** if reflecting it in $l$ gives the same figure; $l$ is an **axis (line) of symmetry**.

cards.title: Reflection in a line
body: $l$ is the perpendicular bisector of $PP'$: right angle at $O$ and $PO = OP'$. $C$ is on the mirror, so $C' = C$.

cards.title: Axes of symmetry
body: Isosceles triangle 1, rectangle 2, regular hexagon 6 (a regular $n$-gon has $n$), circle infinitely many (every diameter). A scalene triangle has none.

cards.title: Reflections on the coordinate plane
body: Use the rule — no drawing needed:
- in the **x-axis**: $(x, y) \to (x, -y)$ (change the sign of $y$)
- in the **y-axis**: $(x, y) \to (-x, y)$ (change the sign of $x$)
- in the line **$y = x$**: $(x, y) \to (y, x)$ (swap)
- in the line **$y = -x$**: $(x, y) \to (-y, -x)$ (swap and change both signs)
- in the **origin** (point reflection): $(x, y) \to (-x, -y)$. $O$ is the midpoint of $PP'$.

**Why $y = x$ swaps:** the midpoint $\left(\frac{x + x'}{2}, \frac{y + y'}{2}\right)$ lies on $y = x$, and $PP'$ has slope $-1$ (perpendicular to slope $1$). Solving the two equations gives $x' = y$, $y' = x$.

cards.title: Five reflections of P(3, 2)
body: $A(3, -2)$ in the x-axis, $B(-3, 2)$ in the y-axis, $C(2, 3)$ in $y = x$, $D(-3, -2)$ in the origin, $E(-2, -3)$ in $y = -x$.

cards.title: Worked example: two reflections, two orders
cards.problem: Reflect $(2, -3)$ in the line $y = -x$ and then in the x-axis. Then do it in the opposite order. Is the result the same?

cards.title: 4.3.2 Translation
body: A **translation** slides every point the **same distance in the same direction**. It is described by where it takes the origin: if $T(0, 0) = (m, n)$ then
- "Translation by $(3, 7)$" means add 3 to $x$ and 7 to $y$.
- If $T$ takes $(a, b)$ to $(c, d)$, then $T$ moves every point by $(c - a, d - b)$; in particular $T(0, 0) = (c - a, d - b)$.
- **Pre-image:** go backwards — subtract: the pre-image of $(4, 9)$ under translation by $(3, 7)$ is $(1, 2)$.
- "1 to the left and 2 down" means translation by $(-1, -2)$.
The image of a figure is congruent to it and points the same way (no flip, no turn).

cards.title: A translation
body: All the arrows $AA'$, $BB'$, $CC'$ are equal and parallel: each point moves 5 right and 3 up.

cards.title: Worked example: find the translation, then use it
cards.problem: A translation takes $(2, 3)$ to $(3, -4)$. Where does it take $(0, 0)$, $(2, -1)$ and $(1, 0)$?

cards.title: Worked example: translate then reflect
cards.problem: Triangle ABC has A(1, 2), B(4, 2), C(1, 5). Translate it by (−3, 1), then reflect the image in the x-axis.

steps.text: Step 1: translate (add −3 to x and 1 to y): A′(−2, 3), B′(1, 3), C′(−2, 6).
Step 2: reflect in the x-axis (change the sign of y): A″(−2, −3), B″(1, −3), C″(−2, −6).
Step 3: both are isometries, so A″B″C″ is congruent to ABC (AB = 3 and A″B″ = 3 ✔).

cards.title: Translate then reflect (the worked example above)
body: Blue: $ABC$. Green: after the translation by $(-3, 1)$. Red: after the reflection in the x-axis. All three triangles are congruent.

cards.title: 4.3.3 Dilation
body: A **dilation** with centre $O$ and **scale factor** $r > 0$ maps each point $P$ to the point $P'$ on ray $OP$ with $OP' = r \cdot OP$. Then every length is multiplied by $r$: $P_1'P_2' = r \cdot P_1P_2$.
- $r > 1$: **expansion** (enlargement), the figure grows.
- $0 < r < 1$: **contraction** (reduction), a scale model.
- $r = 1$: every point stays where it is (a rigid motion).
Angles do not change, so the image is **similar** to the original. Areas are multiplied by $r^2$.
**With centre at the origin:** $(x, y) \to (rx, ry)$.
**To draw a dilation:** draw rays from $O$ through each vertex, measure $OA$, mark $A'$ at $r \times OA$ along the ray, then join the images.

cards.title: Worked example: a contraction (Example 4.8)
cards.problem: Triangle $RST$ has $R(-6, -3)$, $S(6, -3)$, $T(0, 6)$. Find its image under the dilation with centre $O(0, 0)$ and scale factor $\frac23$.

steps.text: Centre at the origin, so multiply both coordinates by $\frac23$.

cards.title: Tip: remember the rules by one example
body: Learn every rule on the single point $(3, 2)$: x-axis $(3, -2)$, y-axis $(-3, 2)$, $y = x$ $(2, 3)$, origin $(-3, -2)$. If you forget a rule in the exam, sketch $(3, 2)$ and its mirror image — the picture gives the rule back.

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: The point (−5, 2) is reflected in the line y = x. What is the image?
cards.why: Reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (x, y) → (y, x), so (−5, 2) → (2, −5).

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: A dilation with centre O and factor 3 maps a triangle of area 5 cm² to an image of area…
cards.why: Lengths are multiplied by k = 3 and areas by k² = 9: 5 × 9 = 45 cm².

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: Which transformation does NOT always give a congruent image?
cards.why: Reflections, translations and rotations keep all lengths (isometries). A dilation with k ≠ ±1 changes the size, giving a similar but not congruent image.

glossary.meaning: A solid bounded only by flat polygon faces.
A polyhedron with two congruent parallel bases joined by parallelogram faces.
The figure cut from a solid by a plane parallel to its base.
A polyhedron with one polygon base and triangular faces meeting at the apex.
The common vertex of the lateral faces of a pyramid.
Height of a lateral face of a pyramid, or distance from the vertex of a cone to the edge of its base.
What remains of a pyramid or cone when the top is cut off parallel to the base.
A pyramid with a triangular base (4 triangular faces).
A cross-section of a sphere through its centre.
The ring between two circles with the same centre.
A flat figure that folds into a solid.
F + V − E = 2 for every polyhedron.
The x-coordinate of a point.
The y-coordinate of a point.
One of the four regions into which the axes divide the plane.
A one-to-one mapping of the whole plane onto itself.
The transformation in which the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of every segment PP′.
A line in which a figure is its own mirror image.
A slide of every point by the same distance in the same direction.
Enlargement or reduction from a centre by a scale factor r.
A transformation that keeps all lengths (reflection, translation).

tips.text: Formula: d = √[(x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²] · midpoint = ((x₁+x₂)/2,(y₁+y₂)/2) Pythagoras on the grid. Keep the signs inside the squares — they die anyway.
Euler: F + V − E = 2. Prism (n-gon): F = n + 2, V = 2n, E = 3n. Pyramid: F = V = n + 1, E = 2n.
Distance subtracts and squares (a number); midpoint adds and halves (a point).
Reflection rules on (3, 2): x-axis (3, −2), y-axis (−3, 2), y = x (2, 3), origin (−3, −2).

questions.q: Prism volume?
why: A prism has the same cross-section all along its length, so V = (area of the base) × (height or length).
questions.label: 3. Prism volume?

questions.q: Cylinder volume?
why: A cylinder is a prism with a circular base of area πr², so V = πr²h.
questions.label: 4. Cylinder volume?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

questions.q: Pyramid volume?
why: A pyramid holds one third of the prism with the same base and height: V = ⅓ × base area × height.
questions.label: 5. Pyramid volume?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

questions.q: Sphere surface?
why: The surface area of a sphere of radius r is 4πr² (four times the area of its great circle πr²).
questions.label: 6. Sphere surface?

questions.q: Sphere volume?
why: V = (4/3)πr³. Example: r = 3 cm gives V = (4/3)π(27) = 36π ≈ 113 cm³.
questions.label: 7. Sphere volume?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

questions.q: A net of a cube has how many squares?
questions.answer: 6, attached so they fold without clash.

questions.q: Reflection in y-axis: (3,−2) goes to?

questions.q: Dilate from origin k=3: (2,−1) goes to?
why: A dilation from the origin with factor k multiplies both coordinates by k: (2, −1) → (3·2, 3·(−1)) = (6, −3).

questions.q: Which maps keep length?
questions.answer: Reflection and translation (and rotation, if listed).
why: Reflections, translations and rotations are isometries: they move a figure without changing lengths or angles, so the image is congruent. A dilation (k ≠ ±1) changes lengths.
questions.label: 12. Which maps keep length?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

questions.q: Dilation k=2 multiplies area by?
why: Lengths are multiplied by k = 2, and area is length × length, so area is multiplied by k² = 4.
questions.label: 13. Dilation k=2 multiplies area by?

questions.q: Why midpoint is not distance?
questions.answer: One averages coordinates; the other is Pythagoras.
why: The midpoint formula averages the coordinates to find a point; the distance formula uses Pythagoras to find a length. They answer different questions.
questions.label: 14. Why midpoint is not distance?

questions.q: Cone volume?
why: A cone is a pyramid with a circular base: V = ⅓ × πr² × h.

questions.q: Polyhedron faces are?

questions.q: Distance never negative because?
why: The distance formula adds two squares, which are never negative, and takes the positive square root, so a distance is always ≥ 0.

questions.q: k=1/2 dilation?
why: With k = 1/2 every point moves halfway towards the centre along its ray, so the image is a reduced copy with all lengths halved.
questions.label: 19. k=1/2 dilation?

questions.q: (0,0) to (0,7) distance?
why: The points have the same x, so the distance is the difference of the y-values: |7 − 0| = 7.

why: Answer C: 90°
An angle inscribed in a semicircle stands on a diameter; the central angle is 180°, so the inscribed angle is half of it: 90°.

questions.q: Which set of faces can form a polyhedron?
why: Step 1: a polyhedron needs at least 4 flat faces to close up space.
Step 2: 4 triangles make a tetrahedron (triangular pyramid). A circle is not a polygon.
questions.tip: Count faces first: fewer than 4 can never enclose space.

similar.q: Can a square and four triangles be the faces of a polyhedron?

questions.q: A cylinder is a polyhedron.
why: Step 1: a polyhedron is bounded by flat polygon faces only.
Step 2: a cylinder has a curved lateral surface and circular bases, so it is not a polyhedron.
questions.tip: Any curved surface → not a polyhedron.

similar.q: Is a hexagonal prism a polyhedron?
similar.a: Yes — all 8 faces are flat polygons.

questions.label: 4.1 Practice — solids, nets and views

questions.q: A pentagonal prism: find $F$, $V$, $E$ and verify Euler’s formula.
why: Step 1: prism with $n = 5$: faces $= n + 2 = 7$ (2 bases + 5 lateral faces).
Step 2: vertices $= 2n = 10$ (5 on each base).
Step 3: edges $= 3n = 15$ (5 + 5 on the bases, 5 lateral).
questions.tip: Prism with $n$-gon base: $F = n + 2$, $V = 2n$, $E = 3n$.
questions.label: 4.1 Practice — solids, nets and views

questions.q: A polyhedron has 8 faces and 6 vertices. How many edges?
why: Step 1: $F + V - E = 2$.
questions.tip: Put the two numbers you know into $F + V - E = 2$ and solve.

similar.q: A polyhedron has 6 faces and 12 edges. How many vertices?

questions.label: 4.1 Practice — solids, nets and views

questions.q: A regular square pyramid has base edge 10 cm and slant height 13 cm. Find its height.
why: Step 1: right triangle with hypotenuse = slant height 13 and one leg = half the base edge 5.
questions.tip: Height, half-edge and slant height form a right triangle; the slant height is the hypotenuse.

similar.q: Base edge 16 cm, height 6 cm. Slant height?

why: Step 2: $l = 13$ cm.
questions.tip: Slant height is always the hypotenuse.

why: Step 2: $t = 8$ cm.
questions.tip: Draw the right triangle: sphere radius is the hypotenuse.

similar.q: Where is the cross-section of largest area?
similar.a: Through the centre ($s = 0$): a great circle.

questions.q: Which arrangement of 6 squares is NOT a net of a cube?

options.A: A row of 4 with one square above and one below
options.D: A row of 3, then a row of 3 shifted by 2

why: Step 1: fold a row of 4: the 4 squares go round the cube.
Step 2: squares 5 and 6 of a straight row would land on the same faces as squares 1 and 2 — the top and bottom stay open.
questions.tip: A cube net never has 5 or more squares in one row.

similar.q: How many different cube nets are there?

questions.label: 4.1 Practice — solids, nets and views

questions.q: Name the solid: front view a triangle, side view a triangle, top view a square with its diagonals.
why: Step 1: top view a square → square base.
Step 2: triangles from the front and side → faces slope up to a point, and the diagonals in the plan are the edges to the apex.
questions.tip: Start with the top view: it shows the shape of the base.

similar.q: Front view rectangle, top view circle?

questions.label: 4.1 Practice — solids, nets and views

questions.q: A cone is to a cylinder as a ____ is to a prism.
why: Step 1: a cylinder and a prism have two equal bases.
Step 2: cutting the top to a point turns a cylinder into a cone and a prism into a pyramid.
questions.tip: Think "two bases" vs "one base and an apex".

similar.q: The part of a cone left after cutting off the top parallel to the base is a …

questions.label: 4.1 Practice — solids, nets and views

questions.q: In which quadrant or on which axis is each point: $(2, 4)$, $(-2, -3)$, $(1, -9)$, $(0, 1)$, $(4, 0)$?
why: Step 1: look at the signs: $(+, +)$ I, $(-, -)$ III, $(+, -)$ IV.
Step 2: a zero coordinate puts the point on an axis: $x = 0$ → y-axis, $y = 0$ → x-axis.
questions.tip: Signs give the quadrant; a zero gives an axis.
questions.label: 4.2 Practice — coordinates, distance and midpoint

questions.q: Find the distance between $(1, -2)$ and $(-3, 4)$.
questions.tip: Square the differences — the minus signs disappear.
questions.label: 4.2 Practice — coordinates, distance and midpoint

questions.q: The distance between $(-3, 2)$ and $(6, 2)$ is
why: Step 1: same $y$ → horizontal segment.
Step 2: distance $= |6 - (-3)| = 9$.
questions.tip: Same $y$: subtract the x’s; same $x$: subtract the y’s.
questions.label: 4.2 Practice — coordinates, distance and midpoint

questions.q: Show that $A(1, 1)$, $B(4, 3)$, $C(4, 1)$ form a right-angled triangle.
why: Step 1: $AC = 3$ (horizontal), $BC = 2$ (vertical), $AB = \sqrt{9 + 4} = \sqrt{13}$.
Step 2: $3^2 + 2^2 = 13 = AB^2$, so the angle at $C$ is $90°$.
questions.tip: Compare the sum of the two smaller squares with the largest square.
questions.label: 4.2 Practice — coordinates, distance and midpoint

questions.q: Show that $(5, -2)$, $(6, 4)$ and $(7, -2)$ are the vertices of an isosceles triangle.
why: Step 3: $(5, -2)$ to $(7, -2)$: $2$. Two sides are equal.
questions.tip: Compute all three sides, then compare.
questions.label: 4.2 Practice — coordinates, distance and midpoint

questions.q: Find the midpoint of $(-6, 5)$ and $(7, 2)$.
why: Step 2: $y = \frac{5 + 2}{2} = \frac72$.
questions.tip: Midpoint = average of the x’s, average of the y’s.
questions.label: 4.2 Practice — coordinates, distance and midpoint

questions.q: The midpoint of a segment is $(3, 2)$ and one endpoint is $(-5, 12)$. Find the other endpoint.
why: Step 1: other end $= (2 \cdot 3 - (-5), 2 \cdot 2 - 12)$.
Step 3: check: average of $-5$ and $11$ is 3; of 12 and $-8$ is 2.
questions.tip: Double the midpoint, subtract the known end.
questions.label: 4.2 Practice — coordinates, distance and midpoint

why: Step 1: slope of the first two: $\frac{3 - 5}{2 - 1} = -2$.
Step 2: slope of the first and third: $\frac{11 - 5}{-2 - 1} = -2$.
Step 3: equal slopes through a common point → collinear.
questions.tip: Collinear = same slope (or the short distances add up to the long one).
questions.label: 4.2 Practice — coordinates, distance and midpoint

questions.q: Show, using coordinates, that the midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right triangle is the same distance from all three vertices.
why: Step 1: put the right angle at $O(0, 0)$, $A(2a, 0)$, $B(0, 2b)$.
Step 2: midpoint of $AB$: $M(a, b)$.
Step 3: $MO = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, $MA = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, $MB = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
questions.tip: Choose easy coordinates: right angle at the origin and the legs on the axes; use $2a$, $2b$ to avoid fractions.

similar.q: What does this tell us about the circle through the three vertices?
similar.a: Its centre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse (the hypotenuse is a diameter).

questions.label: 4.2 Practice — coordinates, distance and midpoint

questions.q: Town M is 36 km east and 15 km north of town N. How far apart are they?
questions.tip: East/north distances are the legs of a right triangle.

similar.q: A point is 8 km east and 6 km south of a town. Distance?

questions.label: 4.2 Practice — coordinates, distance and midpoint

questions.q: Reflect $(4, 5)$ in (i) the x-axis (ii) the y-axis (iii) $y = x$ (iv) $y = -x$ (v) the origin.
why: Step 1: x-axis: change sign of $y$ → $(4, -5)$.
Step 2: y-axis: change sign of $x$ → $(-4, 5)$.
Step 3: $y = x$: swap → $(5, 4)$.
Step 4: $y = -x$: swap and change both signs → $(-5, -4)$.
Step 5: origin: change both signs → $(-4, -5)$.
questions.tip: Learn the five rules on one point and check with a sketch.
questions.label: 4.3 Practice — reflection, translation and dilation

questions.q: Reflect $(6, -3)$ in the x-axis and then reflect the image in the x-axis again.
why: Step 2: $(6, 3) \to (6, -3)$ — back to the start.
questions.tip: Reflecting twice in the same line undoes it.
questions.label: 4.3 Practice — reflection, translation and dilation

questions.q: The image of $(x, y)$ under reflection in the line $y = x$ is
why: Step 1: the line $y = x$ is the perpendicular bisector of $PP'$.
Step 2: this happens exactly when the coordinates are swapped.
questions.tip: Test with $(3, 2)$: its mirror in $y = x$ is $(2, 3)$.
questions.label: 4.3 Practice — reflection, translation and dilation

questions.q: A translation takes the origin to $(-2, 1)$. Where does it take $(2, 1)$, $(-2, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$?
why: Step 1: the rule is $(x, y) \to (x - 2, y + 1)$.
questions.tip: Where the origin goes = what you add to every point.

similar.q: A translation moves every point 1 left and 2 down. Image of $(1, 1)$?

questions.label: 4.3 Practice — reflection, translation and dilation

questions.q: Find the pre-image of $(-3, 4)$ under the translation by $(3, 7)$.
why: Step 1: the translation adds $(3, 7)$, so the pre-image subtracts it.
questions.tip: Pre-image: undo the move.
questions.label: 4.3 Practice — reflection, translation and dilation

questions.q: Find the images of $(4, 7)$, $(-2, 1)$ and $(-5, -4)$ under the translation by $(2, -3)$.
why: Step 1: add 2 to each $x$ and $-3$ to each $y$.
questions.tip: Write the rule $(x + 2, y - 3)$ first.

similar.q: Image of $(0, 0)$ under the same translation?

questions.label: 4.3 Practice — reflection, translation and dilation

questions.q: A dilation with centre $O(0, 0)$ and scale factor 3 maps $A(2, -1)$ to $A'$. Find $A'$ and the ratio $OA' : OA$.
why: Step 1: centre at the origin: multiply coordinates by 3 → $(6, -3)$.
Step 2: $OA' = 3 \cdot OA$, so the ratio is $3 : 1$.
questions.tip: Centre $O$: multiply both coordinates by the scale factor.

similar.q: Image of $(9, -6)$ under the dilation with centre $O$, factor $\frac13$?

questions.label: 4.3 Practice — reflection, translation and dilation

questions.q: A triangle with area 6 cm² is enlarged with scale factor 2. The area of the image is
why: Step 1: lengths are multiplied by $r = 2$.
Step 2: areas are multiplied by $r^2 = 4$: $6 \times 4 = 24$ cm².
questions.tip: Length × $r$, area × $r^2$.

similar.q: Scale factor $\frac12$, original area 20 cm². Image area?

questions.label: 4.3 Practice — reflection, translation and dilation

questions.q: A dilation with scale factor $r \ne 1$ is a rigid motion.
why: Step 1: rigid motions keep all lengths.
Step 2: a dilation multiplies lengths by $r$, so lengths change unless $r = 1$.
questions.tip: Rigid = congruent image; dilation = similar image.

similar.q: Is a translation a rigid motion?
similar.a: Yes — lengths and angles are kept.

questions.label: 4.3 Practice — reflection, translation and dilation

questions.q: How many lines of symmetry: (a) equilateral triangle (b) scalene triangle (c) regular $n$-gon (d) circle?
why: Step 1: equilateral triangle: one through each vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side → 3.
Step 2: scalene: no two sides equal → none.
Step 3: regular $n$-gon: $n$ axes.
Step 4: circle: every diameter is an axis.
questions.tip: Fold the shape in your mind: each fold that matches is one axis.

similar.q: Lines of symmetry of a square?
